stories.summary: Daniel Emhof's report from Molokaʻi recalls how Prince Kūhiō served in Congress and championed the Hawaiian Homes Commission to protect his people.
stories.text: As Molokaʻi Hawaiian homesteaders, we celebrate Hawaiʻi's Prince John Kuhiu Kalanianauli. During his lifetime, and in the decades immediately following his death, Kuhiu was recognized as one of the greatest Hawaiians who had ever lived. Raised as a prince of the royal family in Hawaiʻi, he shrugged off the deep resentment he felt for the overture of the kingdom and ran for election as a territorial delegate, so that he could better defend Hawaiʻi in Washington, D.C., where the big decisions were being made after annexation. He didn't want to leave Hawaiʻi, but look around. He saw that there was no one else to assume the role of protector of his people. It was his kuleana as an aliʻi. It was his duty and his honor and his responsibility. And he championed the Hawaiian Homes Commission, which created the Department of Hawaiian Homelands, which has helped give generations of Hawaiian residents stable homes on the islands, which was designed to provide open area homesteads to Hawaiians who had been dispossessed by ways of changes and the U.S. annexation of the Hawaiian islands in 1898. As Molokai homesteaders, we Continue to carry the kuleana of Prince Janakohi o Kalani ʻAnaole, as you can see today, and the kuleana of our ʻāina, Hoʻopula, Pula, Molokaʻi. And finally, mahalo and enjoy the event as we are mindful of those who came before us and the rich history and outsized impact of an exceptional kanaka, Prince Janakohi o Kalani ʻAnaole.

stories.headline: PSA: native forests provide Hawaiʻi's water supply

stories.text: Here in Hawaiʻi, we're blessed with beautiful native forests found nowhere else on Earth. These forests play a key role in generating our water supply. The water we use and drink comes mainly from rainfall. But because of recent climate changes, Hawaiʻi's rainfall is declining, and we need to take action. The good news is that our native forests of mosses, ferns, and trees have evolved into powerful water-gathering engines that capture moisture from passing clouds and prevent erosion. The bad news is that over half of Hawaiʻi's native forests have already been lost. Non-native animals are demolishing our forests. Non-native weeds choke off their ability to capture water. To help solve these problems, the State Department of Land and Natural Resources is building fences, removing invasive plants and animals, and replanting native forests. We need your help to protect Hawaiʻi for generations to come. To kukua, visit dlnr.hawaii.gov.

stories.text: What we're working on today is a partnership with the Department of Transportation, Keep It Flowing, and Hawaiʻi Partnership to Prevent Underage Drinking, in Awareness of Impaired Driving Prevention. Art gravitates everyone to come together and all the students here, they all just wanted to volunteer their time, even on the weekend. As high schoolers, we're all starting to either want to learn how to drive or are already learning how to drive. And I feel like it's important we know what we should be cautious of. This generation, the education and the awareness can spread so much faster because of their social media use and their way of influencing others. They really have that power and I feel that when they know that about themselves and they will be able to stand firm about saying no, that that will spread to everyone that they're around. A project like this combines beauty, community to make something that is gonna remind us that we can make a difference. Because of what happened with my daughter Azalea, I want to be a part of any project that is spreading the same message that I am. Just hearing the families that went through tragic events and hearing their stories, this is why we're doing it. We want to be able to honor the people who have passed and also we wanted to make sure that we prevent them from happening.

stories.headline: Uncle Sol warns against deep seabed mining
stories.summary: Despite global opposition, the Trump administration is ramping up seabed mining efforts, and Sol Kahoohalahala says the ocean is home and its culture would be destroyed.
stories.text: In our mind, there is no division of the seas. The animals of the sea don't see a boundary Any more than we see a boundary, we have a great ocean of which we are related to and come from and care for, and that's our home. I challenge that perception that culture can only be by tangible artifacts. When we are traveling across the seas at great distances, we are intimate with knowing the currents. We know the waves and their movements, clouds and the weather. We know the resources that are in the deep seas. We are the culture of the people of the deep sea, and our culture is intangible. The ocean is everything to us. It's what we depend upon for our sustenance To think that all the different kinds of creation that is related to the deep sea will be disrupted and then ultimately disrupt potentially the food chain of which now we have subsisted for millennia. In those conversations of mining, there's even no consideration that we come It's about minerals, it's about resources, it's about extraction with no regard for culture. It's that that bothers me about this process of deep sea mining. It's important for us to participate at these kinds of discussions. There is a culture of the deep seas. I want to be a voice of our ancestors. I want to be the one that says, we come from this place. This is our home. And you are now intruding upon it. And so that is an ultimate kind of destruction that should not occur.

stories.text: Have you ever wondered what the ocean provides you? Our oceans support us in so many different ways. They provide us with food, support the economy through tourism, and even provide medicinal products. Even most of the oxygen we breathe is provided by our oceans. Oceans also contain some of the most diverse ecosystems supporting over half of all life on Earth. Hawaii's marine life is so unique many species found here are endemic, meaning they can't be found anywhere else on earth. Our oceans face many threats like marine pollution, reef degradation, and overfishing. Marine pollution comes in many different forms such as pesticides and nutrients used in agriculture. Plastics are also entering oceans at an alarming rate and discarded fishing nets and lines are resulting in animals becoming entangled. Pollution can also be in the form of noise from shipping and drilling. Unsustainable fishing practices and over-harvesting have resulted in a substantial decline in marine species. Coral reefs, which are hot spots for biodiversity, also face multiple threats, including warming ocean temperatures caused by climate change, which can cause coral bleaching and even death. Even our actions when enjoying ocean activities like snorkeling can have a negative impact if not done responsibly. So how can we help protect our oceans? Here are some actions you can take. Reduce your plastic consumption. You can reduce your plastic consumption by replacing single-use plastics with reusable items such as bottles, sandwich bags, straws, and utensils, or by choosing compostable alternatives. And by consuming less plastic, you can reduce your carbon footprint. Practice proper reef etiquette. Remember, the reef is alive. Avoid touching or standing on the reef. And practice proper dive posture. If you need to take a rest, take a stand on the sand. Do not touch, handle, or feed marine life. Species like the Hawaiian green sea turtle and Hawaiian monk seal are protected by law, keeping a safe distance when observing them in their natural habitat. Some chemicals in sunscreens are known to negatively impact marine life. Choose mineral-based sunscreens like zinc oxide and titanium dioxide. Choose sustainably caught seafood. If you like seafood, take some time to research and learn about the food you eat. Many programs like the Monterey Bay Seafood Watch and NOAA's Fish Watch are great resources to help you make more informed, sustainable choices. Thank you for watching this video to help bring awareness to our oceans. We can all play a part in protecting our planet to conserve it for future generations. Well said.

stories.headline: Proposed rule threatens Hawaii's endangered species; invasive species segment
stories.summary: The host warns a proposed Trump rule would remove habitat protection under the Endangered Species Act, then a segment features Molokai Land Trust's director on the invasive species threat and the need for biosecurity.
stories.text: Aloha, my name is Butch Haas. I'm the executive director for the Molokai Land Trust. We're a non-profit conservation organization that was founded in 2006. Since then, we've been working on restoration of the 2,000 acres that we own and manage here on Molokai. The greatest threats that are posed to Hawaiʻi by invasive species are multi-pronged and affect us on many different levels. From an economic standpoint, to a quality of life standpoint, to the basic ecosystem services that we all rely on for survival. I can't express enough how important it is that we stay on top of the invasive species threat here in Hawaiʻi To preserve the unique genetic heritage that makes this spot so incredibly amazing as a genetic hot spot here in the world. Hawaiʻi has been for a long time the endangered species capital of the world due to invasive species. So when we look at preservation of those species, we need to look at heading off new invasive species that are coming into our state on a regular basis. And I'd like to just highlight the Invasive Species Committees and the Hawaiʻi Invasive Species Council for organizing the island-wide Invasive Species Committees. It's so important that we have this support so that we have a first line of defense to respond to initial and immediate threats when they arrive on our island. State and local politicians have a critical role in our battle against invasive species. First and foremost, you are the voice of the public when it comes to this topic. And it is so critical that you understand the dire nature and the threat posed by invasive species so that you can respond in a really appropriate fashion and get the public's attention and trust in responding to these types of threats. One of the very first things that you're going to come across is the environmental and ecological threat ʻOst to our native species, but the public is going to demand more of a response when it comes to the economic threat to our agricultural systems. So the battle against invasive species is a long battle. We have to look at it as the long game, which requires having adequate funding in place to support the first line of defense through our invasive species committees, A strong biosecurity measure through the Department of Agriculture and enforcement measures at our ports of entry and our airports where we have the constant influx of new genetics, new threats coming in on a daily basis. We look at countries across the Pacific and around the world who have taken biosecurity measures seriously and we've traveled to those countries. We understand the efforts that they are taking place on a regular basis, everything from Pumigation of the airplanes when you arrive to searches of all your luggage and really strict enforcement measures for imported items. I feel like when we travel to and from Hawaiʻi we are not seeing this level of biosecurity in place, although we have a biosecurity plan that was recently adopted. I feel like that our politicians really need to step up and enforce the focus on implementing biosecurity measures in a stringent way across the board. Otherwise, we're going to be looking at some dire consequences down the road to just look at history to see how the impacts are both to our economy and to our environment. As a final thought on invasive species, I would just like to remind both our political leaders as well as members of the general public, we are all in this fight together and it's going to take all of us working together to keep what we protected from the threat of invasive species. So, you know, Maybe consider if you as a member of the public, volunteering with a local conservation group, like the Molokai Land Trust, if you're here on Molokai, to come out and work alongside our trained staff on invasive species control and removal, and get a firsthand experience on how we can actually realistically turn the tide against invasive species and restore the incredible genetic heritage that makes Hawaiʻi so special.

stories.headline: Hawaii consumer confidence in serious decline
stories.summary: A new report shows consumer confidence in the islands falling, with people worried about finances, big purchases and jobs.
stories.text: It's the economy in Hawaiʻi that is really shaking people up. A new report reveals that consumer confidence in the islands is in serious decline. People are worried about finances and shying away from big ticket purchases like houses and cars. Many people are worried they may not have a job in six months.

stories.headline: Egg prices climb in Hawaii this year
stories.summary: Since January 1st, local egg prices rose 20% and imported mainland eggs rose 30% amid avian bird flu on the mainland.
stories.text: One economic indicator for everyone is the price of eggs. It is not a dime a dozen, but closer to ten bucks a dozen these days. Avian bird flu on the mainland has scrambled prices, and the price of local and mainland eggs in Hawaiʻi rose significantly in the first quarter of this year. Since January 1st, egg prices rose by 20% for local eggs, while the price of imported mainland eggs rose 30%.

stories.headline: Health insurers may claim part of wildfire settlements
stories.summary: As wildfire victims near settlements, it is unclear whether health insurers will try to claim some of the money, which could be tens or hundreds of thousands per victim.
stories.text: As victims injured in the 2023 Maui wildfires begin to line up to receive legal settlements, a big question looms. Will health insurers who paid for their medical care try to lay claim to some of that money? The answer comes from the state of Maui.

stories.headline: Lahaina community meeting set for Wednesday evening
stories.summary: A Lahaina Community Meeting at 5:30 p.m. April 2 at Lahaina Intermediate School cafeteria will cover recovery updates and be carried live on Akakū Channel 53.
stories.text: Lahaina residents are invited to the Lahaina Community Meeting at 5.30 p.m. tomorrow, Wednesday, April 2nd at Lahaina Intermediate School cafeteria. The meeting will cover updates from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, debris transfer plans from Olauala to central Maui, and Hawaiian Electric's restoration efforts. Residents will also hear about a proposed neighborhood watch program and community feedback on the Community Development Block Grant funding from the Office of Recovery. The meeting will be carried live on Akakū Channel 53 and streamed to the County of Maui Facebook page.

stories.headline: Maui United Way invests $1.5 million in Lahaina land trust
stories.summary: Maui United Way is funding the Lahaina Community Land Trust to keep land in local hands and preserve affordable housing, cultural spaces and ecosystems.
stories.text: Keeping Lahaina lands in Lahaina hands is the mantra of the Lahaina Community Land Trust, and Maui United Way has invested $1.5 million to help the Land Trust protect Lahaina's lands for future generations. The funding supports efforts to keep land in the hands of local residents and preserve affordable housing, cultural spaces, and ecosystems. The initiative also promotes economic development aligned with Lahaina's history and values.

stories.headline: State asks judge to allow vehicles on Olinda Road trail
stories.summary: DLNR has asked Judge Peter Cahill to broaden his March 18th ruling to allow motor vehicle use for firefighting, invasive species control and watershed work.
stories.text: When it comes to keeping public lands public, yesterday we reported a story about opening up a historic trail to the summit of Haleakalā from the top of Olinda Road. State land officials have asked Maui Circuit Court Judge Peter Cahill to broaden his March 18th ruling on the trail to include the use of motor vehicles for certain purposes and projects. The Department The Department of Land and Natural Resources has asked the court to change the injunction, saying the court order limits the use of the trail by preventing their vehicles from driving the route, restrains firefighters from access to the area above Olinda Road in the event of a wildfire, and it affects efforts to control invasive species while maintaining critical watersheds.

stories.headline: Project Keiki returns to Foodland to fight child hunger
stories.summary: From April 1st through April 30th, customers can donate at Foodland stores to support food banks feeding keiki who lose school meals.
stories.text: Nearly one in three children in Hawaiʻi go hungry, with some going entire days without eating. But Project Keiki returns this month to food land stores across the state to support Hawaiʻi's food banks in fighting child hunger. The initiative helps feed Keiki, who lose access to school meals during weekends and school breaks. Beneficiaries include Hawaiʻi Food Bank, the Maui Food Bank and others. From April 1st through April 30th, customers can donate at any Foodland, Sack and Save or Foodland Farms location.

stories.headline: Cigarette tax increase moves in the legislature
stories.summary: A bill would raise the cigarette tax from 16 to 18 cents, with the extra two cents going to Hawaii cancer research.
stories.text: You can smoke them if you can get them, but it is going to cost you. An increase in the cigarette tax is moving in the state legislature. And if approved, this sin tax will jump from 16 to 18 cents. The extra two cents will go to support Hawaiʻi cancer research.

stories.headline: Actor Richard Chamberlain dies a day before his 91st birthday
stories.summary: Longtime Hawaii resident Richard Chamberlain, star of the original Shogun series and Dr. Kildare, has died.
stories.text: The recent FX drama Shogun won several Emmy Awards and widespread acclaim for Maui showrunners Rachel Kondo and Justin Marks. But the star of the original Shogun TV series, longtime Hawaiʻi resident and legendary actor Richard Chamberlain, has died only one day before his 91st birthday. Chamberlain also starred in one of the first medical soaps on television as Dr. Kildare.

stories.headline: Rare white blackfish spotted off Makaha
stories.summary: A pure white blackfish seen off Makaha, Oahu may be the first recorded true albino whale in Hawaiian waters.
stories.text: This is a whale of a tale, and it's no April Fool's joke. A whale species known as blackfish was spotted off Makaha on Oahu on Friday, but the blackfish was pure white. Experts think that it is an extremely rare sighting of an albino pygmy killer whale, the first observation of a true albino whale in Hawaiian waters ever recorded.
